<a name="ai-model-ecosystems-for-artists"></a>
## AI model ecosystems for artists

### Basic Identification

**Name:** AI model ecosystems for artists
**Type:** tool
**Originator:** Key people, organizations, or communities behind this item

Stability AI (Emad Mostaque, Stable Diffusion 2022). Midjourney (David Holz, 2022). OpenAI (DALL-E, 2021). RunwayML (Cristobal Valenzuela, Alejandro Matamala, 2018). ComfyUI (comfyanonymous, 2023). Community: Civitai for model sharing, Hugging Face for open models. LoRA technique from Microsoft Research.

**Year:** 2022 (mass adoption breakout with Stable Diffusion and Midjourney)
**Key Url:** https://stability.ai/
**Geography:** Where it operates, originates, or is concentrated

Global. Stability AI (London), Midjourney (San Francisco), OpenAI (San Francisco), RunwayML (New York). Open-source community is globally distributed. Strong adoption in US, Europe, East Asia, South America.


### Core Ideas & Positioning

**Core Claim:** The central proposition or value claim this item makes

Generative AI models enable artists to create images, video, audio, and 3D content through natural language prompts and visual controls, fundamentally expanding who can create and how. The ecosystem spans closed commercial platforms (Midjourney, DALL-E) to fully open-source systems (Stable Diffusion + ComfyUI) offering maximum customization and control.

**Medium Specificity:** What makes this digitally native? What is specific to digital art about this item vs. art generally?

Entirely digitally native. These tools create new forms of computational image-making where the model's latent space becomes a creative medium. The specificity is in the prompt-to-image translation, the ability to traverse latent spaces, fine-tune models on specific aesthetics (LoRA), and build complex generation pipelines (ComfyUI workflows). This is not simulation of traditional media but a new mode of image production.

**Relation To Attention Economy:** How does this item relate to attention logic? Does it optimize for engagement, resist it, or ignore it?

Deeply entangled. Social media virality drives adoption (Midjourney images dominate visual social media). The ease of generation creates an attention surplus: more images produced than can receive meaningful attention. Platform design (Midjourney's Discord gallery, Civitai trending models) optimizes for engagement. The speed of generation rewards prolific posting over contemplative practice. However, the open-source ecosystem (Stable Diffusion, ComfyUI) enables private, non-performative use that escapes attention logic.

**Relation To Intention:** Does this serve declared structural needs (intention) or capture engagement (attention)? Or is it infrastructure-neutral?

Dual nature. The tools can serve intention (artists using AI as a medium for deliberate creative practice) or attention (mass generation for social media engagement, content farm production). The ecosystem does not inherently favor either. Midjourney's curation of aesthetic quality suggests some intention-alignment, while the ease of generation and social sharing mechanics pull toward attention capture. The artist's choice of tool and practice determines alignment.


### Market & Economic Dimensions

**Revenue Model:** How it sustains itself financially. Primary sale, secondary royalties, subscription, grants, token, none.

Midjourney: subscription ($10-60/month). DALL-E: credit-based via ChatGPT Plus ($20/month). RunwayML: subscription with generation credits. Stable Diffusion: free (open-source), but GPU costs for local running or cloud compute fees. ComfyUI: 100% free and open-source. Civitai: freemium model marketplace. The open-source ecosystem enables zero-cost entry with hardware investment only.

**Market Position:** Primary market, secondary market, infrastructure, tool, none. Where in the value chain.

Tool layer with emerging platform characteristics. Midjourney operates as a walled garden. Stable Diffusion + ComfyUI is open infrastructure. RunwayML bridges creative tools and AI. The market is bifurcating between convenience (closed platforms) and control (open-source).


### Practice & Aesthetic Dimensions

**Toolchain:** Primary tools, languages, platforms used. What software/hardware enables this practice?

Stable Diffusion (model) + ComfyUI (workflow) + ControlNet (spatial control) + LoRA (style fine-tuning) + IPAdapter (image guidance) is the power-user stack. Midjourney via Discord. DALL-E via ChatGPT. RunwayML for video. Civitai and Hugging Face for model discovery. Local deployment requires NVIDIA GPUs (8GB+ VRAM minimum, 24GB recommended). Cloud alternatives: ThinkDiffusion, Replicate, fal.ai.

**Relation To Ai:** How it engages with (or resists) generative AI. Tool, medium, subject, threat, irrelevant.

This IS the AI art tool layer. The central tension is between AI as tool (artist retains creative agency, uses AI as one element in a broader practice) and AI as autonomous creator (text prompt in, finished image out). The ecosystem increasingly supports the tool model: ControlNet for precise spatial control, LoRA for stylistic specificity, ComfyUI for complex multi-step workflows. However, the dominant use case remains prompt-to-image generation where AI makes most creative decisions.

**Liveness:** Static artifact, real-time, performative, evolving, generative, interactive.

Primarily static artifact generation, but evolving toward: real-time generation (Stable Diffusion turbo models), interactive installations (camera-to-generation pipelines), live performance (real-time style transfer), and video generation. ComfyUI workflows can be real-time and interactive. The ecosystem is moving from batch artifact production to real-time generative systems.

**Aesthetic Vocabulary:** What critical/aesthetic language exists for describing this? Is the vocabulary adequate or still forming?

Rapidly developing but contested. Prompt engineering, latent space, diffusion, denoising, CFG scale, LoRA, checkpoint, safetensors, ControlNet, inpainting, outpainting, img2img, txt2img, seed, sampler, negative prompt. Critical vocabulary is less developed: 'AI slop' (pejorative for generic AI output), 'AI art' (contested term), 'co-creation,' 'human-AI collaboration.' The field lacks adequate critical language to distinguish between superficially similar AI outputs with vastly different artistic intention and process.

**Tendency Axis Position:** Position on A(DAI) tendency axes: openness↔enclosure, commons↔capture, spectacle↔infrastructure, individual↔collective

Bifurcated. Open-source ecosystem (Stable Diffusion, ComfyUI): strongly open, commons-oriented, infrastructure-focused. Closed platforms (Midjourney, DALL-E): enclosed, capture-oriented, spectacle-focused. The field as a whole trends toward individual production (prompt-to-image) rather than collective practice. The open-source side contributes significantly to commons; the closed side encloses.


### Infrastructure & Governance

**Openness:** Open-source, proprietary, hybrid, CC-licensed. What is shared and what is enclosed?

Spectrum. Stable Diffusion: open-source (various licenses, SDXL is open). ComfyUI: GPL. Flux models: open weights. LoRA/fine-tuning techniques: openly published. Midjourney: fully closed, no local running. DALL-E: closed API only. RunwayML: proprietary with API access. The open-source side is genuinely open; the commercial side is genuinely closed. This bifurcation is the ecosystem's defining structural feature.

**Governance Model:** Who decides what. DAO, curatorial, corporate, community, founding-team, expert-committee, none.

Stability AI: corporate (venture-backed, troubled governance, CEO departures). Midjourney: small team, founder-led, opaque decision-making. OpenAI: corporate with nonprofit origins (much-debated governance). ComfyUI: community-driven, founder-led open-source project. The governance landscape is fragmented with no industry coordination on standards, ethics, or interoperability.

**Data Sovereignty:** Who owns/controls the data, art, metadata? Can artists export their data? Is it portable?

Critical weakness. Most models were trained on data scraped from the internet without artist consent (LAION-5B dataset). Artists have limited ability to remove their work from trained models. Closed platforms retain generated outputs on their servers. Open-source tools enable local generation with no data leaving the user's machine. The training data consent crisis is the ecosystem's most significant ethical challenge.

**Interoperability:** Can it connect to other systems/platforms? Standards compliance. API availability. Graph-readiness.

Growing within the open ecosystem. ComfyUI nodes can integrate models from different sources. Safetensors format is a shared model distribution standard. LoRAs and ControlNet modules work across compatible models. However, Midjourney, DALL-E, and RunwayML are walled gardens with no cross-platform workflow. The open-source ecosystem is highly interoperable; the commercial ecosystem is fragmented.

**Preservation Strategy:** How permanence is addressed. On-chain, IPFS, institutional archive, none, at-risk.

Open models and weights can be preserved as files. ComfyUI workflows are saved as JSON, enabling reproduction. Generated images are standard files. However, the rapid model evolution means specific outputs may be irreproducible as models are superseded. No systematic archival of AI art tools or outputs exists. Closed platform outputs are at-risk if platforms shut down.

**Consent Architecture:** How consent is managed. Binary include/exclude, granular, machine-readable, absent.

The ecosystem's deepest structural failure. Most training datasets were compiled without creator consent. Spawning/HaveIBeenTrained provides opt-out infrastructure but adoption by AI companies is voluntary. Stability AI and Hugging Face agreed to honor Spawning's do-not-train registry. Midjourney and OpenAI's consent architecture is opaque. The EU AI Act and various lawsuits are forcing consent infrastructure development, but it remains inadequate.


### Field Position & Gaps

**Relation To Traditional Art World:** Integration, parallel, opposition, absorption, indifference. How does it sit relative to galleries/museums/fairs?

Contested integration. Major galleries and auction houses have exhibited and sold AI art (Refik Anadol at MoMA, Christie's AI art sales). Art fairs increasingly include AI-generated work. However, significant resistance from traditional artists and critics who question authorship, skill, and artistic merit. Photography's historical struggle for acceptance is often cited as a parallel. The 2023 Washtington Post-viral Colorado State Fair AI art controversy crystallized the debate.

**What It Enables:** What becomes possible because of this? What can practitioners do that they couldn't before?

Visual creation accessible to non-artists (democratization or deskilling, depending on perspective). Rapid iteration and prototyping for professional artists. New aesthetic possibilities exploring latent spaces. Custom model training for specific styles or subjects. Complex multi-step generation pipelines (ComfyUI). Video and 3D content generation. AI-assisted art that combines human and machine creativity in novel ways.

**What It Lacks:** What's missing, broken, or structurally absent from this item?

Consent infrastructure for training data. Clear attribution models for AI-assisted work. Critical frameworks adequate to evaluate AI art beyond novelty or technical prowess. Tools for artists to understand what their models have learned and from whom. Mechanisms for compensating artists whose work contributed to model training. Preservation strategies for AI art practice documentation. The ability to trace specific outputs to training data influences.

**Who Is Excluded:** Who can't participate and why? Technical barriers, geographic barriers, economic barriers, cultural barriers.

Artists without GPU hardware or cloud compute budgets (for open-source). Artists in regions with restricted internet access. Artists whose consent was violated by training data scraping (they are involuntary participants, not excluded, but their agency is denied). Artists whose aesthetic vocabulary was homogenized by model biases. Non-English speakers face reduced prompt effectiveness. Blind and visually impaired artists are excluded from visual-generation tools. Communities whose visual culture is underrepresented in training data receive poor generation quality.

**Frontier Signal:** Is this emerging (frontier), established, or declining? If frontier: what category does it challenge?

Frontier across the board. Video generation (Sora, Runway Gen-3, Kling), 3D generation, real-time generation, multi-modal models, and custom model training are all active frontiers. The challenge is shifting from what AI can generate to what it should generate and how authorship, consent, and attribution should function. The technology is ahead of the ethical and institutional frameworks.


### Attention & Intention Dynamics

**Discovery Mechanism:** How people find this. Algorithm, curation, word of mouth, institutional, search, social media, none.

Social media (Twitter/X, Reddit, YouTube tutorials), Discord communities, Civitai model marketplace trending lists, word of mouth, tech journalism, YouTube channels (Stability AI official, ComfyUI tutorials), conference presentations. Discovery is heavily social-media-driven.

**Attention Dependency:** How dependent on platform attention/engagement metrics? Would it survive if Twitter/Instagram disappeared?

High for commercial platforms. Midjourney's growth was entirely social-media-driven (Discord virality). Stable Diffusion's adoption was driven by Reddit, Twitter, and YouTube coverage. If social media disappeared, the tools would persist but adoption would slow dramatically. The open-source ecosystem has more resilient discovery through GitHub, documentation, and community forums.

**Intention Alignment:** Does it serve declared structural needs of the field or capture engagement? Intention-native, attention-native, neutral.

Mixed. The tools can serve artistic intention (fine-tuned models for specific practices, ComfyUI workflows for controlled generation) or attention capture (mass generation for social media, content farming). The ecosystem's defaults favor ease and volume over deliberation and meaning. Artists who use these tools intentionally must actively resist the pull toward attention-optimized production.

**Commons Contribution:** Does it contribute to shared field knowledge (open data, shared vocabulary, public infrastructure) or enclose it?

Bifurcated. Open-source ecosystem: massive commons contribution through shared models, workflows, tutorials, techniques. Civitai, Hugging Face, and ComfyUI communities exemplify open knowledge sharing. Closed platforms: minimal commons contribution, enclosed proprietary systems. The training data crisis undermines commons claims: open models built on unconsented data are extractive commons that take from artists without reciprocity.


### Provenance & Temporality

**Provenance Type:** What kind of provenance does this track? Ownership only, meaning, both, neither.

Neither, primarily. Generated outputs typically have no provenance tracking. Some platforms embed C2PA metadata (Content Credentials) for AI-generated content detection, but this is provenance of origin (was this AI-made?) rather than provenance of ownership or meaning. The training data provenance (what data influenced this output?) is technically impossible to reconstruct from a generated image.

**Temporal Logic:** Real-time, archival, cyclical/tidal, anticipatory, deep-historical, none.

Primarily anticipatory (what can we generate next?) and real-time (generation as live process). No deep-historical awareness. Model versions replace each other rapidly. The ecosystem is presentist, focused on the latest model capabilities rather than understanding or preserving its own short history.

**Absence Handling:** Does this item detect, represent, or address what is missing from the field? Or only what is present?

Significant absences are structural but unacknowledged. Training data biases create systematic absences: visual cultures not represented in LAION-5B produce poor generation quality. The consent of artists whose work trained the models is absent. Documentation of artistic process (beyond final outputs) is largely absent. The ecosystem does not represent or address its own gaps.


### Coherence & Contestability

**Coherence Vs Consensus:** Does this seek consensus (single truth), coherence (multiple valid readings coexist), or neither?

Neither coherence nor consensus. The field is in active, unresolved conflict. Is AI art real art? Is prompting creative authorship? Should training data require consent? Is open-source AI democratizing or enabling exploitation? These questions have no coherent shared framework, let alone consensus. Different communities (AI artists, traditional artists, ethicists, technologists, lawyers) operate with incompatible values.

**Contestability:** Can outputs, classifications, or judgments be challenged? By whom? Through what mechanism?

High. Every aspect of the ecosystem is actively contested: authorship, consent, quality, value, legality, ethics. Ongoing lawsuits (Getty v. Stability AI, Andersen v. Stability AI et al.) are contesting fundamental legal questions. The USCO's guidance on AI copyrightability represents institutional contestation. Artists contest through tools (Glaze, Nightshade) and advocacy (Spawning). The ecosystem is defined by contestation.

**Forkability:** Can this be forked — taken, modified, and run independently? What are the practical barriers?

High for open-source components. Stable Diffusion has been forked numerous times. ComfyUI is forkable. LoRAs and custom models are inherently forkable. Closed platforms (Midjourney, DALL-E) cannot be forked. The bifurcation between forkable and non-forkable mirrors the open/closed divide.


### A(DAI) Comparison

**Layer Mapping:** none
**What Adai Should Adopt:** Specific patterns, methods, or principles A(DAI) should learn from this item.

The open-source ecosystem's commons-first model building approach. ComfyUI's node-based workflow architecture as a model for composable, transparent processes. The community-driven model sharing and improvement culture. The recognition that tools shape practice and must be understood to map the field. The principle that infrastructure should be transparent and auditable.

**What Adai Should Refuse:** What A(DAI) must explicitly refuse from this item's approach.

The training data consent violation as a foundational practice. The attention-optimized production model that prioritizes volume over meaning. The presentist temporal logic that discards its own history. The aesthetic homogenization that results from shared model biases. The conflation of generation with creation. The enclosure of knowledge by closed platforms. The disregard for artist agency and livelihood.

**Structural Tension:** The productive tension between this item's approach and A(DAI)'s architecture.

AI model ecosystems are the fastest-evolving layer of the digital art field, yet they are also the most ethically contested and the least historically self-aware. A(DAI) must track this layer rigorously (it is reshaping practice, markets, and discourse simultaneously) while maintaining critical distance from its attention-optimized values. The tension is between the need to understand AI's impact on the field and the refusal to normalize consent violations and aesthetic homogenization as acceptable costs of innovation.


### Regulatory & Legal Environment

**Ip Model:** How intellectual property is handled. CC license, all-rights-reserved, on-chain ownership, public domain, mixed.

Deeply contested. Model weights: various open licenses (Apache 2.0, custom licenses). Generated outputs: no copyright protection for fully AI-generated works (US, as of 2025). Human-AI collaborative works: case-by-case determination of sufficient human authorship. Training data: claimed as fair use by AI companies, contested by artists and rights holders in court. LoRAs trained on specific artists' work raise unresolved IP questions.

**Opt In Vs Opt Out:** Is consent opt-in (explicit) or opt-out (must actively refuse)? Neither? What are the implications?

Predominantly opt-out, which is the core ethical failure. Training data was collected without consent. Artists must actively opt out (via Spawning, robots.txt, platform-specific mechanisms) rather than being asked to opt in. The EU AI Act and ongoing litigation may force a shift toward opt-in, but this has not occurred yet. Spawning's Source.Plus represents an emerging opt-in model for ethical training data.


### Ecosystem Position

**Platform Dependency:** What platforms, chains, or services does this depend on? Single point of failure risk.

Varies dramatically. Midjourney: complete dependency on Midjourney Inc. and Discord. DALL-E: dependent on OpenAI. Stable Diffusion: distributed, no single dependency (models downloadable, multiple UIs). ComfyUI: open-source, no platform dependency. All GPU-dependent workflows depend on NVIDIA (market dominance in AI-capable GPUs). Cloud services create dependency on compute providers.

**Network Effects:** Does this benefit from or contribute to network effects? Is it a hub, bridge, or isolate?

Strong. Midjourney benefits from community gallery and shared prompt knowledge. Civitai's model marketplace has strong network effects (more models attract more users attract more model creators). ComfyUI's node ecosystem benefits from developer network effects. Training data itself represents a controversial network effect: more data creates better models creates more users creates more data. Open-source model sharing creates positive-sum network effects.

**Post Crash Trajectory:** Specific trajectory since 2022-2023 crash. Growing, stable, declining, pivoting, dead.

Growing rapidly, independent of NFT crash. The AI art tool ecosystem was nascent during the NFT boom (Stable Diffusion launched August 2022, after NFT peak). The trajectory is exponential adoption with ongoing ethical/legal reckoning. The market is splitting between professional creative tools (RunwayML for filmmakers) and consumer-accessible generation (Midjourney, DALL-E). The open-source ecosystem is the fastest-growing segment.

<a name="archival-gap-for-born-digital-works"></a>
## Archival gap for born-digital works

### Basic Identification

**Name:** Archival gap for born-digital works
**Type:** gap
**Originator:** Key people, organizations, or communities behind this item

Systemic failure across institutions. Partial responses from Rhizome (ArtBase, Webrecorder/Conifer), Le Random, Library of Congress, Smithsonian, NARA, Yale Born Digital Archives Group

**Year:** Year founded, launched, or emerged

Ongoing since the emergence of net art in the 1990s. Increasingly acute since 2021 NFT boom produced millions of on-chain works with no preservation strategy

**Key Url:** https://rhizome.org/editorial/2024/aug/14/introducing-rhizomes-preservation-services/
**Geography:** Where it operates, originates, or is concentrated

Global gap. Preservation efforts concentrated in North America (Rhizome, Smithsonian, Library of Congress) and Europe (ZKM, V&A). Near-zero preservation infrastructure in Global South, Asia, Africa


### Core Ideas & Positioning

**Core Claim:** The central proposition or value claim this item makes

The digital art field is producing work faster than it can preserve. No field-wide preservation strategy exists. Born-digital works depend on platforms, blockchains, storage services, and software formats that may not persist. The archival gap is a deep-time infrastructure failure — the field risks losing its own history as it creates it.

**Medium Specificity:** What makes this digitally native? What is specific to digital art about this item vs. art generally?

Born-digital works face unique preservation challenges absent in traditional media: software dependency (works break when browsers, operating systems, or plugins update), platform dependency (works hosted on centralized platforms disappear when platforms close), chain dependency (NFTs depend on blockchain infrastructure and IPFS/Arweave pinning), format obsolescence (proprietary formats become unreadable), and interactivity (preserving behavior, not just appearance, requires emulation or migration).

**Relation To Attention Economy:** How does this item relate to attention logic? Does it optimize for engagement, resist it, or ignore it?

The attention economy actively works against preservation. Platforms optimize for new content, not archival access. Social media algorithms bury older work. NFT marketplaces prioritize trending collections over historical significance. The economic incentives are entirely misaligned with long-term preservation — attention accrues to the new, not the enduring.

**Relation To Intention:** Does this serve declared structural needs (intention) or capture engagement (attention)? Or is it infrastructure-neutral?

Preservation is deeply intention-aligned. It serves the long-term structural needs of the field (maintaining its history, enabling future scholarship, preserving artistic legacy) rather than capturing engagement. The gap represents a fundamental failure of intentional infrastructure — the field has built market infrastructure but not memory infrastructure.


### Market & Economic Dimensions

**Revenue Model:** How it sustains itself financially. Primary sale, secondary royalties, subscription, grants, token, none.

Preservation has no revenue model. Rhizome operates on grants (Mellon Foundation, NEA) and institutional support (New Museum affiliation). Le Random is venture-funded with permanent capital structure. Smithsonian and NARA are government-funded. No market mechanism funds preservation. The costs are real (storage, emulation development, staff time) but no buyer or collector directly pays for archival access.

**Market Position:** Primary market, secondary market, infrastructure, tool, none. Where in the value chain.

Infrastructure — entirely outside the market value chain. Preservation creates long-term cultural value but generates no transactional revenue.


### Practice & Aesthetic Dimensions

**Toolchain:** Primary tools, languages, platforms used. What software/hardware enables this practice?

Key preservation tools: Rhizome Conifer (web archiving), Webrecorder (browser-based archiving), Emulation-as-a-Service (running legacy software), IPFS and Arweave (decentralized storage), Wikibase/Linked Open Data (metadata management). File format standards: OAIS reference model, PREMIS metadata, Dublin Core. Blockchain-specific: on-chain storage, IPFS pinning services, Arweave permaweb.

**Relation To Ai:** How it engages with (or resists) generative AI. Tool, medium, subject, threat, irrelevant.

AI could potentially assist preservation through automated format detection, migration path recommendation, and metadata extraction. However, AI-generated art creates additional preservation challenges — prompts, model weights, training data, and generation parameters are part of the work but rarely preserved alongside outputs. No established standard for preserving AI art provenance exists.

**Liveness:** Static artifact, real-time, performative, evolving, generative, interactive.

The preservation gap is most acute for live, interactive, and generative works. Static images and videos can be preserved using established techniques. But works that involve real-time computation, user interaction, network connections, or evolving generative processes require fundamentally different approaches (emulation, re-implementation) that are technically complex and expensive.

**Aesthetic Vocabulary:** What critical/aesthetic language exists for describing this? Is the vocabulary adequate or still forming?

The vocabulary for discussing digital art preservation is borrowed from library science and archival studies (bit-level preservation, migration, emulation, fixity). It lacks art-specific language for describing what is lost when a work is partially preserved — the aesthetic, experiential, and relational dimensions of loss are not captured by technical preservation terminology.

**Tendency Axis Position:** Position on A(DAI) tendency axes: openness↔enclosure, commons↔capture, spectacle↔infrastructure, individual↔collective

Commons over capture (preservation is inherently a commons activity). Infrastructure over spectacle (archiving is invisible work). Openness over enclosure (Rhizome's tools are open-source). Collective over individual (preservation serves the field, not individual market interests).


### Infrastructure & Governance

**Openness:** Open-source, proprietary, hybrid, CC-licensed. What is shared and what is enclosed?

Mixed. Rhizome's tools (Conifer, Webrecorder) are open-source. The ArtBase uses Linked Open Data via Wikibase. NARA publishes its Digital Preservation Framework on GitHub. But many institutional preservation systems are proprietary. On-chain storage (IPFS, Arweave) is open infrastructure but depends on economic incentives (pinning costs, token economics) for persistence.

**Governance Model:** Who decides what. DAO, curatorial, corporate, community, founding-team, expert-committee, none.

Fragmented. No single governing body for born-digital art preservation. Each institution makes independent decisions. Rhizome leads through technical innovation. NARA and Library of Congress set government standards. No equivalent of ICOM (International Council of Museums) specifically for digital art preservation.

**Data Sovereignty:** Who owns/controls the data, art, metadata? Can artists export their data? Is it portable?

Critical issue. Artists often lose control of their work's preservation. Platform-hosted works are preserved (or not) at the platform's discretion. On-chain works depend on blockchain and storage layer persistence. Rhizome's ArtBase preserves works with artist consent but artists cannot self-serve. No standard for artist-controlled preservation exists.

**Interoperability:** Can it connect to other systems/platforms? Standards compliance. API availability. Graph-readiness.

Low across the field. Different institutions use different metadata standards, storage systems, and preservation approaches. Rhizome's use of Linked Open Data and Wikibase is an exception that enables interoperability. No universal standard connects institutional archives, on-chain metadata, and marketplace records.

**Preservation Strategy:** How permanence is addressed. On-chain, IPFS, institutional archive, none, at-risk.

This IS the preservation strategy gap. Partial strategies exist: Rhizome (emulation, web archiving, LOD), Smithsonian (bit-level preservation, migration, emulation), on-chain community (IPFS, Arweave). But no field-wide strategy coordinates these efforts or addresses the scale of the problem.


### Field Position & Gaps

**Relation To Traditional Art World:** Integration, parallel, opposition, absorption, indifference. How does it sit relative to galleries/museums/fairs?

The traditional art world has centuries of preservation infrastructure (museums, climate-controlled storage, conservation labs). Born-digital art has almost none of this. Institutional absorption of digital art (e.g., museums acquiring NFTs) does not solve the problem because museums lack technical preservation capacity for software-based works.

**What It Enables:** What becomes possible because of this? What can practitioners do that they couldn't before?

When functional, preservation enables: art historical scholarship, exhibition of historical works, understanding of artistic lineage and influence, protection of cultural heritage, and long-term value maintenance for collectors.

**What It Lacks:** What's missing, broken, or structurally absent from this item?

Field-wide coordination. Standardized metadata for preservation. Artist-controlled preservation mechanisms. Preservation infrastructure for interactive and generative works. Economic models to fund perpetual preservation. Integration between on-chain provenance and institutional archives. Preservation infrastructure for works on non-Ethereum chains (Tezos, Solana, etc.).

**Who Is Excluded:** Who can't participate and why? Technical barriers, geographic barriers, economic barriers, cultural barriers.

Artists on smaller or less-established blockchains. Artists whose work depends on centralized platforms that may close. Artists without institutional connections who cannot access Rhizome or museum preservation programs. Artists in the Global South where no preservation infrastructure exists. Artists working in ephemeral or performance-based digital media.

**Frontier Signal:** Is this emerging (frontier), established, or declining? If frontier: what category does it challenge?

Established as a recognized problem but frontier as a solution space. Rhizome's 2024 Preservation Services launch and the growth of Emulation-as-a-Service represent frontier infrastructure. The challenge of preserving AI-generated art is entirely frontier territory with no established approaches.


### Attention & Intention Dynamics

**Discovery Mechanism:** How people find this. Algorithm, curation, word of mouth, institutional, search, social media, none.

Institutional channels, academic conferences (DigiCAM25, Archiving 2025), specialist publications. Preservation work is largely invisible to the broader art world and public. Discovery is limited to those already embedded in preservation communities.

**Attention Dependency:** How dependent on platform attention/engagement metrics? Would it survive if Twitter/Instagram disappeared?

Very low attention dependency. Preservation work continues regardless of public attention. However, funding for preservation depends partly on public awareness of the problem, creating a paradox: the work is invisible by nature but needs visibility to secure resources.

**Intention Alignment:** Does it serve declared structural needs of the field or capture engagement? Intention-native, attention-native, neutral.

Maximally intention-aligned. Preservation serves the deepest structural need of any cultural field: maintaining access to its own history. This is pure infrastructure work with no attention-capture component.

**Commons Contribution:** Does it contribute to shared field knowledge (open data, shared vocabulary, public infrastructure) or enclose it?

Potentially the highest commons contribution of any activity in the field. Preserved works become part of shared cultural heritage. Open-source tools (Conifer, Webrecorder) contribute to preservation commons. Linked Open Data approaches enable interoperable knowledge. But the contribution is unrealized at scale due to the infrastructure gap.


### Provenance & Temporality

**Provenance Type:** What kind of provenance does this track? Ownership only, meaning, both, neither.

The gap affects both ownership and meaning provenance. On-chain provenance tracks ownership but not context, interpretation, or significance. Institutional archives track some meaning provenance (exhibition history, critical reception) but this is not linked to on-chain records. The preservation gap means both types of provenance are at risk of loss.

**Temporal Logic:** Real-time, archival, cyclical/tidal, anticipatory, deep-historical, none.

Deep-historical. Preservation operates on a timescale of decades to centuries. The gap is between the field's production tempo (real-time, continuous) and its preservation tempo (near-zero for most works). This temporal mismatch is the core structural failure.

**Absence Handling:** Does this item detect, represent, or address what is missing from the field? Or only what is present?

This item IS about absence — the systematic loss of born-digital works over time. The gap detects absence (we know works are being lost) but cannot address it at scale. No mechanism exists to even inventory what has already been lost.


### Coherence & Contestability

**Coherence Vs Consensus:** Does this seek consensus (single truth), coherence (multiple valid readings coexist), or neither?

Neither. Preservation approaches are fragmented without shared principles. Different institutions prioritize different aspects (Rhizome emphasizes access, Smithsonian emphasizes bit-level integrity, on-chain community emphasizes permanence through decentralization). No coherence framework connects these approaches.

**Contestability:** Can outputs, classifications, or judgments be challenged? By whom? Through what mechanism?

Low. Preservation decisions (what to preserve, how to preserve it, what fidelity is acceptable) are made by individual institutions without external review or challenge mechanisms. Artists cannot contest how their work is preserved or whether it is preserved at all.

**Forkability:** Can this be forked — taken, modified, and run independently? What are the practical barriers?

Moderate. Open-source tools (Conifer, Webrecorder) can be forked and deployed independently. But preservation requires ongoing institutional commitment, not just software — forking the tools does not fork the organizational capacity to maintain archives over decades.


### A(DAI) Comparison

**Layer Mapping:** substrate
**What Adai Should Adopt:** Specific patterns, methods, or principles A(DAI) should learn from this item.

A(DAI) should adopt the principle that intelligence infrastructure must include preservation by design, not as an afterthought. Every signal, node, and relationship in A(DAI) should be durably stored with preservation metadata. A(DAI) should learn from Rhizome's Linked Open Data approach (Wikibase) for interoperable, machine-readable preservation. A(DAI) should also learn from the LOCKSS principle (Lots of Copies Keep Stuff Safe) and build redundancy into its storage architecture.

**What Adai Should Refuse:** What A(DAI) must explicitly refuse from this item's approach.

A(DAI) should refuse platform-dependent storage without fallback. It should refuse to build on any single storage layer (IPFS alone, a single cloud provider) without redundancy. It should refuse the assumption that blockchain permanence equals preservation — on-chain data persists but may become inaccessible without context, tooling, and maintained interfaces.

**Structural Tension:** The productive tension between this item's approach and A(DAI)'s architecture.

A(DAI) operates at the level of meaning and context; preservation infrastructure operates at the level of bits and formats. The tension is between preserving the physical artifact (the file, the code, the blockchain record) and preserving the meaning (the context, the interpretation, the relational significance). A(DAI) could bridge this by building meaning-layer preservation alongside bit-level preservation.


### Regulatory & Legal Environment

**Ip Model:** How intellectual property is handled. CC license, all-rights-reserved, on-chain ownership, public domain, mixed.

Complex. Preservation requires copying, which implicates copyright. Institutional archives typically operate under fair use or specific legal exemptions. On-chain works have varied IP terms (some CC0, some all-rights-reserved). No standardized IP framework for digital art preservation exists.

**Opt In Vs Opt Out:** Is consent opt-in (explicit) or opt-out (must actively refuse)? Neither? What are the implications?

Mostly opt-in for institutional programs (artists submit to Rhizome ArtBase). Opt-out is the default for on-chain works — they are publicly visible but not actively preserved unless someone takes action. No mechanism for artists to signal preservation preferences.


### Ecosystem Position

**Platform Dependency:** What platforms, chains, or services does this depend on? Single point of failure risk.

High and dangerous. Works hosted on centralized platforms (galleries, marketplaces, social media) are entirely dependent on those platforms' continued operation and preservation decisions. Works on IPFS depend on pinning services continuing to operate. Works on Arweave depend on the Arweave network's long-term viability. Even on-chain works depend on blockchain infrastructure remaining accessible.

**Network Effects:** Does this benefit from or contribute to network effects? Is it a hub, bridge, or isolate?

Negative network effects for preservation. As more works are produced, the preservation backlog grows. Each new platform, chain, or format creates additional preservation complexity. The network effect of production works against the capacity for preservation.

**Post Crash Trajectory:** Specific trajectory since 2022-2023 crash. Growing, stable, declining, pivoting, dead.

The 2022-2023 crash exposed preservation vulnerabilities. Platforms that closed (e.g., various NFT marketplaces) took hosted metadata and media with them. IPFS-hosted works with unpaid pinning became inaccessible. The crash demonstrated that market infrastructure is not preservation infrastructure. Post-crash: growing institutional awareness of the problem, Rhizome's 2024 Preservation Services launch, Le Random's permanent collection model, but the gap continues to widen.

<a name="arena"></a>
## Are.na

### Basic Identification

**Name:** Are.na
**Type:** infrastructure
**Originator:** Key people, organizations, or communities behind this item

Charles Broskoski (co-founder, product), Daniel Pianetti (operations), Damon Zucconi (engineering), Meg Miller (editorial). Original team included Dena Yago and John Michael Boling.

**Year:** 2011
**Key Url:** https://www.are.na/
**Geography:** Where it operates, originates, or is concentrated

New York City based. Global user community, heavily concentrated among digital art practitioners, designers, researchers, and cultural workers in North America and Europe.


### Core Ideas & Positioning

**Core Claim:** The central proposition or value claim this item makes

A collaborative knowledge-curation platform that enables deep, interconnected research without algorithmic manipulation. Anti-engagement-metric, anti-advertising, subscription-funded. The closest thing to commons knowledge infrastructure for digital art practitioners.

**Medium Specificity:** What makes this digitally native? What is specific to digital art about this item vs. art generally?

Digitally native in its curation model: blocks (content units) can exist in multiple channels simultaneously, creating a non-hierarchical web of associations. This many-to-many relational structure is impossible in physical curation. The platform treats content as research material rather than social media posts.

**Relation To Attention Economy:** How does this item relate to attention logic? Does it optimize for engagement, resist it, or ignore it?

Explicitly resistant. Are.na deliberately avoids algorithmic feeds, push notifications, video-centric engagement, ads, and AI integrations. Discovery is user-driven through search and channel following. The platform positions itself as a refuge from attention-economy platforms. A 2024 podcast described it as 'the Good Web.' Monthly recurring revenue of $114K (2025) demonstrates that an anti-attention business model can sustain itself, if modestly.

**Relation To Intention:** Does this serve declared structural needs (intention) or capture engagement (attention)? Or is it infrastructure-neutral?

Strongly intention-native. Are.na serves declared structural needs: collaborative research, knowledge organization, and community-driven curation. It explicitly refuses to capture engagement or optimize for attention. The subscription model aligns incentives -- the platform serves the user, not advertisers.


### Market & Economic Dimensions

**Revenue Model:** How it sustains itself financially. Primary sale, secondary royalties, subscription, grants, token, none.

Freemium subscription. Free tier with limited blocks; paid subscription for unlimited blocks and premium features. Monthly recurring revenue: $114,302 as of 2025. Total expenses: $106,522. No advertising. No venture capital (equity crowdfunding in 2018 with 850 investors, ~75% existing members). Deliberately no-VC to maintain mission alignment.

**Market Position:** Primary market, secondary market, infrastructure, tool, none. Where in the value chain.

Infrastructure/tool. Not a marketplace. Serves as the knowledge-curation layer that practitioners use alongside other platforms. Complementary to rather than competing with art marketplaces.


### Practice & Aesthetic Dimensions

**Toolchain:** Primary tools, languages, platforms used. What software/hardware enables this practice?

Web platform (are.na), API (v2, v3 in development), browser extensions for collecting content. Blocks support text, images, links, embedded media, PDFs. Channels as organizational units. Nested channels for hierarchical structures.

**Relation To Ai:** How it engages with (or resists) generative AI. Tool, medium, subject, threat, irrelevant.

Explicitly resistant. Are.na deliberately avoids AI integrations to preserve user agency and community harmony. This is a principled stance against the attention-economy dynamics that AI-powered features typically introduce. However, this also means Are.na cannot offer AI-assisted research, semantic search, or automatic connection-finding.

**Liveness:** Static artifact, real-time, performative, evolving, generative, interactive.

Static curation with social dynamics. Content is manually curated; channels evolve over time through collaborative addition. No real-time, generative, or automated components.

**Aesthetic Vocabulary:** What critical/aesthetic language exists for describing this? Is the vocabulary adequate or still forming?

Are.na contributes vocabulary around knowledge curation and research practice: blocks, channels, connections, collaborative research, anti-algorithmic design. The platform itself has a distinctive minimal aesthetic that signals its anti-spectacle values. It does not define art-critical vocabulary but provides infrastructure for developing and sharing such vocabulary.

**Tendency Axis Position:** Position on A(DAI) tendency axes: openness↔enclosure, commons↔capture, spectacle↔infrastructure, individual↔collective

Strongly openness-leaning (channels are public by default, knowledge is shared). Commons-native (subscription-funded, no enclosure of user data for advertising). Infrastructure over spectacle (deliberately anti-flashy). Collective over individual (collaborative channels, shared research).


### Infrastructure & Governance

**Openness:** Open-source, proprietary, hybrid, CC-licensed. What is shared and what is enclosed?

Hybrid. Channels are public by default (can be made private). API available. No open-source codebase. Content is accessible but the platform infrastructure is proprietary. Exploring cooperative ownership models.

**Governance Model:** Who decides what. DAO, curatorial, corporate, community, founding-team, expert-committee, none.

Founding-team governed with community orientation. No formal community governance mechanism. The 2018 crowdfunding created ~850 investor-members but no structured governance rights. Exploring cooperative or public benefit corporation transition. The editorial team (Meg Miller) provides curatorial direction.

**Interoperability:** Can it connect to other systems/platforms? Standards compliance. API availability. Graph-readiness.

Limited. API (v2) provides access to channels and blocks. No support for linked data standards, knowledge graph protocols, or structured metadata interoperability. Content can be imported via browser extension but export is limited. Not graph-ready for external systems.

**Preservation Strategy:** How permanence is addressed. On-chain, IPFS, institutional archive, none, at-risk.

Platform-dependent. No decentralized storage, no blockchain preservation. The Annual book provides some physical archival of community output. Content persists as long as Are.na operates. No redundancy or backup mechanism for the knowledge graph.

**Consent Architecture:** How consent is managed. Binary include/exclude, granular, machine-readable, absent.

Basic. Channels can be public, private, or collaboration-only. Block-level privacy is limited. No granular consent for how content is connected or recontextualized when blocks appear across multiple channels. No machine-readable consent standards.


### Field Position & Gaps

**Relation To Traditional Art World:** Integration, parallel, opposition, absorption, indifference. How does it sit relative to galleries/museums/fairs?

Parallel but connected. Used by practitioners and students across art schools and cultural institutions. The 2015 Guggenheim collaboration (Azone Futures Market) demonstrated institutional recognition. Not a market player but a research companion to traditional art practice.

**What It Enables:** What becomes possible because of this? What can practitioners do that they couldn't before?

Collaborative visual and textual research across distributed communities. Non-hierarchical knowledge organization. A space for slow, deep thinking about art and culture without algorithmic pressure. Cross-pollination between disciplines through shared channels.

**What It Lacks:** What's missing, broken, or structurally absent from this item?

Structured semantic relations between blocks (connections are implicit, not typed). No knowledge graph functionality. No search beyond keyword matching (no semantic or conceptual search). Limited export and interoperability. No formal ontology or taxonomy. The knowledge is socially organized but not machine-readable.

**Frontier Signal:** Is this emerging (frontier), established, or declining? If frontier: what category does it challenge?

Established with frontier potential. The platform itself is mature (13 years) but the model it represents -- anti-algorithmic, subscription-funded, commons-oriented -- is increasingly relevant as a counter-model to AI-driven platforms. The cooperative transition would be genuinely frontier for a platform of this type.


### Attention & Intention Dynamics

**Discovery Mechanism:** How people find this. Algorithm, curation, word of mouth, institutional, search, social media, none.

User-driven: search, channel following, browsing connected channels. Word of mouth. Editorial (Are.na Annual). No algorithmic recommendation. No push notifications. Discovery requires active exploration.

**Attention Dependency:** How dependent on platform attention/engagement metrics? Would it survive if Twitter/Instagram disappeared?

Very low. Are.na's survival does not depend on platform attention metrics. It would survive if Twitter/Instagram disappeared -- its user base finds it through institutional recommendations, word of mouth, and direct search. The subscription model insulates it from attention-economy fluctuations.

**Intention Alignment:** Does it serve declared structural needs of the field or capture engagement? Intention-native, attention-native, neutral.

Strongly intention-native. The platform exists to serve knowledge curation and collaborative research. No engagement optimization, no advertising, no data extraction. The subscription model ensures the user is the customer, not the product.

**Commons Contribution:** Does it contribute to shared field knowledge (open data, shared vocabulary, public infrastructure) or enclose it?

Significant in practice, limited in structure. Are.na hosts enormous amounts of shared knowledge (public channels on art, design, culture). But this knowledge is not structured, not machine-readable, and not exportable as a knowledge graph. The commons contribution is social rather than infrastructural -- it exists within Are.na's walls rather than as open data.


### Provenance & Temporality

**Provenance Type:** What kind of provenance does this track? Ownership only, meaning, both, neither.

Neither ownership nor meaning formally. Blocks have timestamps and attribution. Channel curation history is visible. But there is no provenance tracking in the art-world sense.

**Temporal Logic:** Real-time, archival, cyclical/tidal, anticipatory, deep-historical, none.

Archival (content persists) with social temporality (channels evolve over time through community additions). The Annual publication introduces a cyclical editorial temporality.

**Absence Handling:** Does this item detect, represent, or address what is missing from the field? Or only what is present?

Does not explicitly address absence. However, the open channel model allows communities to surface gaps -- users can create channels around what is missing, underrepresented, or overlooked. This is emergent rather than designed.


### Coherence & Contestability

**Coherence Vs Consensus:** Does this seek consensus (single truth), coherence (multiple valid readings coexist), or neither?

Coherence by design. Multiple channels can contain the same block with different contextualizations. No single authority on how content should be classified. The platform enables diverse readings to coexist without forcing consensus.

**Contestability:** Can outputs, classifications, or judgments be challenged? By whom? Through what mechanism?

Informal. Users can create alternative channels that reframe content differently. There is no formal contestation mechanism, but the open channel structure allows dissenting perspectives to exist alongside dominant ones. Community norms are soft rather than codified.

**Forkability:** Can this be forked — taken, modified, and run independently? What are the practical barriers?

Low forkability at the platform level (proprietary code). High forkability at the content level -- any user can create a new channel that reframes or recontextualizes existing blocks. However, forking the entire platform would require rebuilding the social graph and community, which is the primary value.


### A(DAI) Comparison

**Layer Mapping:** sensing-loop
**What Adai Should Adopt:** Specific patterns, methods, or principles A(DAI) should learn from this item.

The anti-algorithmic, subscription-funded model as proof that intention-native platforms can survive financially. The many-to-many block-to-channel model (content existing in multiple contexts simultaneously) as a pattern for relational knowledge. The collaborative research ethos. The Annual publication as a model for periodic synthesis. The cooperative ownership exploration.

**What Adai Should Refuse:** What A(DAI) must explicitly refuse from this item's approach.

The lack of structured semantic relations. Are.na's connections are implicit and social, not typed or machine-readable. A(DAI) needs the relational depth that Are.na lacks: typed edges, ontological structure, graph-readiness. Also refuse the closed codebase and limited interoperability. Are.na proves the social model works but does not solve the infrastructure problem.

**Structural Tension:** The productive tension between this item's approach and A(DAI)'s architecture.

Are.na demonstrates that anti-algorithmic knowledge curation has a viable community and business model. A(DAI) wants the same ethos but with structured graph infrastructure underneath. The tension is between Are.na's social looseness (which enables serendipity and creative freedom) and A(DAI)'s need for structured relations (which enable machine reasoning and cross-system interoperability). Can you add structure without killing the organic quality?


### Regulatory & Legal Environment

**Regulatory Exposure:** Which regulations apply? EU AI Act, AB 2013, DMCA, copyright opt-out regimes. How does this item comply or conflict?

Minimal. Standard web platform regulations. GDPR compliance for European users. No AI Act exposure (no AI features). No crypto/blockchain regulatory exposure. Privacy-first design reduces regulatory surface area.

**Ip Model:** How intellectual property is handled. CC license, all-rights-reserved, on-chain ownership, public domain, mixed.

User-owned content. Are.na does not claim IP over user-contributed blocks. Content licensing depends on what users share (links, images, text). No platform-level license assertion beyond terms of service.

**Opt In Vs Opt Out:** Is consent opt-in (explicit) or opt-out (must actively refuse)? Neither? What are the implications?

Opt-in. Users choose to create accounts, contribute blocks, and join channels. Public channels are visible to all but participation requires account creation. No opt-out needed because there is no algorithmic tracking or data extraction to opt out of.


### Ecosystem Position

**Platform Dependency:** What platforms, chains, or services does this depend on? Single point of failure risk.

Self-hosted web platform with standard cloud infrastructure. No blockchain dependency. No marketplace dependency. The primary dependency is on the community itself -- if the community migrates, the platform's value collapses.

**Network Effects:** Does this benefit from or contribute to network effects? Is it a hub, bridge, or isolate?

Moderate positive network effects. More users create more channels, making the platform more valuable for research. However, the anti-growth stance limits the scale of these effects. The network is deep (highly engaged users) rather than broad (mass adoption).

**Post Crash Trajectory:** Specific trajectory since 2022-2023 crash. Growing, stable, declining, pivoting, dead.

Not directly affected by NFT crash as Are.na is not a crypto/NFT platform. Steady growth throughout 2022-2025. The crash may have benefited Are.na by driving practitioners away from speculative platforms toward research-oriented ones. Revenue growing modestly; expenses covered. The platform's position strengthens as attention-economy fatigue grows.
