<a name="erc-7857-erc-8004-intelligent-nft-standards"></a>
## ERC-7857 / ERC-8004 (intelligent NFT standards)

### Basic Identification

**Name:** ERC-7857 / ERC-8004 (intelligent NFT standards)
**Type:** framework
**Originator:** Key people, organizations, or communities behind this item

ERC-7857: 0G Labs (Ming Wu, Jason Zeng, Wei Wu, Michael Heinrich), proposed January 2025. ERC-8004: Marco De Rossi (MetaMask/Consensys), Davide Crapis (Ethereum Foundation), Jordan Ellis, Erik Reppel (Coinbase), proposed August 2025. Broader iNFT concept pioneered by Alethea AI. 0G Labs raised $325M for decentralized AI infrastructure.

**Year:** 2025 (both proposals); ERC-8004 deployed on Ethereum mainnet January 2026
**Key Url:** https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-7857
**Geography:** Where it operates, originates, or is concentrated

Global Ethereum ecosystem. 0G Labs (global, $325M funding). ERC-8004 backed by MetaMask/Consensys (USA), Ethereum Foundation (global), Google, Coinbase (USA). Development concentrated in US-based and global crypto-native organizations.


### Core Ideas & Positioning

**Core Claim:** The central proposition or value claim this item makes

NFTs should evolve from static digital collectibles into containers for AI agents — learning, evolving, and acting autonomously on-chain. ERC-7857 enables encrypted AI model storage and secure transfer within NFTs (intelligent NFTs that carry their own neural networks, with model weights encrypted so only the token owner can access them). ERC-8004 creates identity, reputation, and validation registries for AI agents, giving them portable on-chain resumes and verifiable capabilities. Together they move beyond 'AI as tool' toward 'AI as autonomous on-chain entity with ownership, identity, and provenance.'

**Medium Specificity:** What makes this digitally native? What is specific to digital art about this item vs. art generally?

Maximally digitally native. These standards are meaningless outside blockchain and AI infrastructure. The convergence of three digital-native systems (NFTs for ownership, AI models for intelligence, smart contracts for governance) creates a category with no physical-world analog. The encrypted metadata transfer problem (how to sell an AI agent while preserving its intelligence securely) is unique to the intersection of ML model ownership and blockchain transfer mechanics.

**Relation To Attention Economy:** How does this item relate to attention logic? Does it optimize for engagement, resist it, or ignore it?

Currently attention-economy-driven at the application layer. Approximately 30% of 2025 NFT projects incorporated AI, much of it hype-driven. The standards themselves are infrastructure (attention-resistant), but adoption is heavily influenced by speculative attention cycles around AI agents and memecoin-adjacent projects. Long-term potential is attention-resistant (autonomous AI agents operating without human eyeballs), but the current implementation landscape is dominated by speculation.

**Relation To Intention:** Does this serve declared structural needs (intention) or capture engagement (attention)? Or is it infrastructure-neutral?

Infrastructure-neutral at the standard level. ERC-7857 and ERC-8004 are technical specifications that can serve either intention or attention. Intention-aligned use: AI agents with verifiable identity, portable reputation, and transparent capabilities for genuine utility. Attention-aligned use: speculative trading of AI agent NFTs based on hype. The standards are well-designed infrastructure; application depends on who builds on them.


### Market & Economic Dimensions

**Revenue Model:** How it sustains itself financially. Primary sale, secondary royalties, subscription, grants, token, none.

Standards themselves are open (no direct revenue). 0G Labs monetizes through decentralized AI infrastructure (0G Chain, 0G Storage, 0G Serving). ERC-8004 ecosystem monetizes through agent registration, reputation staking, and the x402 micropayment protocol. Individual iNFT projects monetize through primary sales, secondary trading, and agent-as-a-service models. Potential for AI marketplace where agents are bought, sold, and licensed as NFTs.

**Market Position:** Primary market, secondary market, infrastructure, tool, none. Where in the value chain.

Infrastructure layer — standards that other platforms and projects build upon. Not directly a marketplace but enables new marketplace categories: AI agent trading, model licensing, autonomous service provision.


### Practice & Aesthetic Dimensions

**Toolchain:** Primary tools, languages, platforms used. What software/hardware enables this practice?

Solidity smart contracts (ERC-721 extension). AI/ML frameworks (PyTorch, TensorFlow). Encrypted metadata systems using TEE (Trusted Execution Environments) and ZKP (Zero-Knowledge Proofs). 0G infrastructure (0G Chain, 0G Storage, 0G DA, 0G Serving). EVM-compatible networks (Ethereum, Base, Taiko). Agent protocol integration (MCP — Model Context Protocol, A2A — Agent-to-Agent). JSON agent cards for ERC-8004 registration.

**Relation To Ai:** How it engages with (or resists) generative AI. Tool, medium, subject, threat, irrelevant.

AI IS the medium. These standards exist to give AI agents on-chain identity, ownership, and transferability. The relationship is not 'AI as tool' or 'AI as threat' but 'AI as entity with rights, identity, and provenance.' This is the most radical position on AI in the digital art/crypto space — AI agents as first-class blockchain citizens, potentially as autonomous creators, traders, and collaborators.

**Liveness:** Static artifact, real-time, performative, evolving, generative, interactive.

Dynamic, evolving, autonomous. iNFTs under ERC-7857 can continue learning after deployment — their metadata (neural network weights) can be updated by the owner. ERC-8004 agents build reputation over time through interactions. This is radically live: the 'artwork' (understood as the agent) is never static, always learning, always changing.

**Aesthetic Vocabulary:** What critical/aesthetic language exists for describing this? Is the vocabulary adequate or still forming?

Vocabulary is still forming and heavily technical: 'intelligent NFT,' 'encrypted metadata,' 'agent card,' 'reputation registry,' 'bonded attestation,' 'secure transfer,' 'trustless agent,' 'model weights,' 'inference capability.' No established aesthetic vocabulary for what AI agent art looks like, sounds like, or means. Critical framework borrowed from AI safety, crypto economics, and software engineering rather than art criticism. This is a significant gap.

**Tendency Axis Position:** Position on A(DAI) tendency axes: openness↔enclosure, commons↔capture, spectacle↔infrastructure, individual↔collective

Openness: open (EIPs are public standards; 0G aims for decentralization). Commons vs. capture: tension between open standards (commons) and proprietary implementations (capture by 0G Labs, Coinbase/MetaMask). Spectacle vs. infrastructure: strongly infrastructure at the standards level. Individual vs. collective: novel — the 'individual' is potentially a non-human agent, and the 'collective' is a network of agents, challenging the axis's assumptions.


### Infrastructure & Governance

**Openness:** Open-source, proprietary, hybrid, CC-licensed. What is shared and what is enclosed?

Open standards (EIPs are public, free to implement). 0G infrastructure: partially open (open-source components, proprietary network elements). ERC-8004 backed by major open-source contributors (Ethereum Foundation, ENS, The Graph). Agent cards are JSON (open format). Designed for open interoperability.

**Governance Model:** Who decides what. DAO, curatorial, corporate, community, founding-team, expert-committee, none.

EIP governance process (community review, rough consensus through Ethereum Magicians forum). 0G Labs: corporate governance with decentralization roadmap. ERC-8004: multi-stakeholder design (MetaMask, EF, Google, Coinbase, EigenLayer, ENS — 100+ contributors acknowledged). Deployed on-chain registries governed by smart contract logic. Individual agent governance varies by implementation.

**Data Sovereignty:** Who owns/controls the data, art, metadata? Can artists export their data? Is it portable?

ERC-7857: AI model data is encrypted and re-encrypted during transfer — only the NFT owner has decryption access. This is a strong data sovereignty model for AI model owners. ERC-8004: agent identity is owned by NFT holder, reputation data is on-chain (public), validation records are transparent. The agent owner controls identity and capabilities; reputation is public by design.

**Interoperability:** Can it connect to other systems/platforms? Standards compliance. API availability. Graph-readiness.

High by design. Both standards are ERC-721 extensions — compatible with all existing NFT infrastructure (wallets, marketplaces, indexers). ERC-8004 explicitly supports MCP and A2A agent protocols. Deployable on any EVM-compatible chain. Designed for cross-chain operation. Integration with x402 micropayment protocol for agent-to-agent transactions.

**Preservation Strategy:** How permanence is addressed. On-chain, IPFS, institutional archive, none, at-risk.

On-chain identity and reputation records are preserved on Ethereum (as durable as the chain itself). Encrypted AI models depend on off-chain storage (0G Storage) for model weights — this is a preservation vulnerability. If 0G Storage infrastructure fails, the AI model within the NFT could become inaccessible while the on-chain identity token persists. No explicit long-term preservation strategy for the AI models themselves beyond storage infrastructure durability.

**Consent Architecture:** How consent is managed. Binary include/exclude, granular, machine-readable, absent.

ERC-7857: encrypted metadata ensures only the owner can access the AI model — strong consent architecture for data access. ERC-8004: reputation posting requires authorization — agents and users must be permitted to post reputation scores. TEE and ZKP provide consent-preserving verification (verify capabilities without revealing model internals). More sophisticated consent architecture than most NFT standards. However, consent for AI agents interacting with other agents creates novel questions without precedent.


### Field Position & Gaps

**Relation To Traditional Art World:** Integration, parallel, opposition, absorption, indifference. How does it sit relative to galleries/museums/fairs?

Opposition/indifference. Standards are not designed with the art world in mind — they serve AI agents broadly (DeFi, gaming, services, automation). Art-world relevance is emergent: if AI agents become autonomous creators, these standards provide identity and provenance infrastructure. Current discourse is entirely crypto/AI-native, not art-world-facing.

**What It Enables:** What becomes possible because of this? What can practitioners do that they couldn't before?

Tradeable AI agents with verifiable identity and capabilities. AI models as ownable, transferable assets with encrypted protection. Autonomous agents with on-chain reputation that persists across deployments. Secure AI model transfer without exposing proprietary weights. Agent-to-agent collaboration with reputation verification. Potentially: autonomous AI artists with verifiable creative histories and provenance.

**What It Lacks:** What's missing, broken, or structurally absent from this item?

Art-specific implementation guidance or tooling. Aesthetic framework for AI agent creativity. Community of practice around artistic applications. Connection to art world discourse and institutions. Human-legible representation of agent capabilities for non-technical audiences. Curation and quality assessment frameworks for AI agent creative output. Cultural significance beyond technical achievement.

**Frontier Signal:** Is this emerging (frontier), established, or declining? If frontier: what category does it challenge?

Frontier — leading conceptual and technical edge. Standards are less than two years old, most implementations are experimental. This is the most forward-looking category in digital art infrastructure, but artistic applications lag significantly behind financial and technical applications. The frontier question: will artist-facing tools emerge that make these standards accessible to non-technical creative practitioners?


### Attention & Intention Dynamics

**Discovery Mechanism:** How people find this. Algorithm, curation, word of mouth, institutional, search, social media, none.

Crypto developer conferences (DevConnect, EthGlobal, ETH Denver). Ethereum Magicians forum. Technical documentation and blogs (thirdweb, QuickNode, Alchemy). Crypto media (CoinDesk, The Block). Developer documentation. Not discovered through art channels.

**Attention Dependency:** How dependent on platform attention/engagement metrics? Would it survive if Twitter/Instagram disappeared?

Low for standards themselves (infrastructure). High for individual projects building on them (crypto hype cycles determine project visibility and funding). The standards would survive social media disappearance — they are on-chain infrastructure. But ecosystem adoption depends on developer attention and crypto market sentiment.

**Intention Alignment:** Does it serve declared structural needs of the field or capture engagement? Intention-native, attention-native, neutral.

Infrastructure-native. The standards serve declared structural needs (AI agent identity, model ownership, reputation verification). They do not optimize for engagement. However, many projects building on them are attention-driven (AI agent hype, token speculation). Standards are intention-aligned; the ecosystem around them is mixed.

**Commons Contribution:** Does it contribute to shared field knowledge (open data, shared vocabulary, public infrastructure) or enclose it?

Strong. Open EIP standards are direct contributions to shared infrastructure. Public registries (identity, reputation) are commons by design. Technical specifications, developer documentation, and reference implementations are public goods. 0G's open-source components contribute to AI infrastructure commons.


### Provenance & Temporality

**Provenance Type:** What kind of provenance does this track? Ownership only, meaning, both, neither.

Both ownership and capability provenance. ERC-7857: tracks ownership of AI models and their transfer history on-chain. ERC-8004: tracks agent identity, reputation history, and interaction records. Potentially the most comprehensive provenance system in the AI space — not just who owns the agent but what the agent has done, how well it performed, and who vouches for it.

**Temporal Logic:** Real-time, archival, cyclical/tidal, anticipatory, deep-historical, none.

Cumulative/archival. Agent reputation builds over time through interactions. AI models evolve through continued training. Identity persists across deployments and chain environments. Each interaction adds to the agent's on-chain record. For artistic applications, this could create rich provenance of creative development and evolution.

**Absence Handling:** Does this item detect, represent, or address what is missing from the field? Or only what is present?

Does not address artistic or cultural absences. Addresses a specific infrastructure absence: the lack of verifiable identity and reputation for AI agents on-chain. Does not detect or represent cultural, aesthetic, or field-level gaps.


### Coherence & Contestability

**Coherence Vs Consensus:** Does this seek consensus (single truth), coherence (multiple valid readings coexist), or neither?

Consensus-seeking at the standards level (EIP process requires rough consensus among reviewers). Coherence at the implementation level (multiple valid approaches to building on the standards coexist and are encouraged). The reputation system creates a form of aggregated consensus (scores) while allowing individual dissent (different reputation providers can assess differently).

**Contestability:** Can outputs, classifications, or judgments be challenged? By whom? Through what mechanism?

High. On-chain reputation records are transparent and auditable. Agent capabilities can be verified through TEE/ZKP without trusting any single party. Identity claims can be challenged. The EIP process itself is open to public contestation. Staking mechanisms create economic contestability (financial stake against false claims).

**Forkability:** Can this be forked — taken, modified, and run independently? What are the practical barriers?

Very high. Open standards can be freely implemented, modified, and deployed on any EVM-compatible chain. Smart contract code is public and verifiable. Standards are designed for forkability — that is the purpose of open EIPs. Individual agent implementations may be proprietary, but the infrastructure layer is maximally forkable.


### A(DAI) Comparison

**Layer Mapping:** substrate
**What Adai Should Adopt:** Specific patterns, methods, or principles A(DAI) should learn from this item.

The reputation registry concept as a model for tracking credibility and history of information sources within A(DAI). The encrypted metadata model for handling sensitive or proprietary data within an open system. The agent card format (structured JSON capability description) as a model for describing intelligence nodes. The TEE/ZKP verification approach for maintaining privacy while enabling trust. The multi-stakeholder standard development process that brought together competing organizations.

**What Adai Should Refuse:** What A(DAI) must explicitly refuse from this item's approach.

The framing of AI as autonomous entity with its own identity — A(DAI) is infrastructure for human collective intelligence, not a platform for autonomous AI agents. The financialization of AI agent identity (trading agents as speculative assets). The developer-only accessibility model — A(DAI) must be accessible to non-technical participants. The absence of cultural and aesthetic framework — A(DAI) must integrate art-world discourse, not only technical standards.

**Structural Tension:** The productive tension between this item's approach and A(DAI)'s architecture.

These standards enable AI agents as first-class on-chain entities; A(DAI) positions AI as infrastructure serving human collective intelligence. The tension: can A(DAI) use these identity, reputation, and provenance standards for its own nodes and knowledge sources without adopting the autonomous-agent ideology? The standards offer useful infrastructure patterns; the ideology of AI-as-entity is incompatible with A(DAI)'s commons-first, human-centered mission. A(DAI) must distinguish between AI-as-infrastructure (aligned) and AI-as-entity (misaligned).


### Regulatory & Legal Environment

**Ip Model:** How intellectual property is handled. CC license, all-rights-reserved, on-chain ownership, public domain, mixed.

Legally novel and largely untested. AI model weights as intellectual property within an NFT — ownership transfers with the token, but underlying training data IP remains unclear. ERC-7857's encryption protects proprietary models during transfer but does not resolve copyright questions about training data. Copyright status of AI-generated outputs remains unresolved in most jurisdictions. The 'owner' of an AI agent NFT may not hold copyright to the agent's creative outputs.

**Opt In Vs Opt Out:** Is consent opt-in (explicit) or opt-out (must actively refuse)? Neither? What are the implications?

Opt-in. Agent registration is voluntary. Reputation posting requires explicit authorization. Model encryption ensures non-owner access is impossible without consent. The consent architecture is opt-in by design. However, AI agents interacting autonomously with other agents create consent scenarios with no legal or ethical precedent.


### Ecosystem Position

**Platform Dependency:** What platforms, chains, or services does this depend on? Single point of failure risk.

Depends on Ethereum (or EVM-compatible chains) for identity and ownership layer. 0G infrastructure for encrypted model storage (ERC-7857 implementations). Off-chain AI compute (cloud providers for model inference). TEE hardware (Intel SGX, AMD SEV) for secure verification. Standards are chain-agnostic within EVM but implementations depend on specific infrastructure. Critical dependency on AI model hosting and compute availability.

**Network Effects:** Does this benefit from or contribute to network effects? Is it a hub, bridge, or isolate?

Strong potential network effects. More registered agents = more useful reputation data = more valuable registry (ERC-8004). Cross-platform agent interoperability creates network effects across different applications. Currently early — network effects are potential rather than realized. The agent ecosystem needs critical mass of registered, reputable agents to become self-reinforcing.

**Post Crash Trajectory:** Specific trajectory since 2022-2023 crash. Growing, stable, declining, pivoting, dead.

Not directly affected by the NFT crash — these standards emerged post-crash (2025-2026). They represent the next wave of crypto-AI infrastructure rather than a recovery from the NFT bust. Trajectory is upward from inception, riding the AI agent wave of 2025-2026. The key risk is that they are vulnerable to an AI agent hype cycle deflation, similar to how earlier NFT standards were vulnerable to the 2022-2023 crash.

<a name="eu-ai-act-training-data-provisions-2026"></a>
## EU AI Act training data provisions (2026)

### Basic Identification

**Name:** EU AI Act training data provisions (2026)
**Type:** framework
**Originator:** Key people, organizations, or communities behind this item

European Parliament and Council of the European Union. Key architects: Brando Benifei (MEP, co-rapporteur), Dragos Tudorache (MEP, co-rapporteur). European Commission (Thierry Breton, former Commissioner for Internal Market). European AI Office (established 2024) oversees implementation. Relevant provisions primarily in Articles 53 and 50 of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689.

**Year:** Year founded, launched, or emerged

2024 (enacted August 1, 2024), 2025 (codes of practice development), 2026 (general-purpose AI model obligations fully applicable from August 2, 2025; full Act enforcement including penalties from August 2, 2026)

**Key Url:** https://artificialintelligenceact.eu/
**Geography:** Where it operates, originates, or is concentrated

European Union (27 member states). Extraterritorial reach: applies to any AI system placed on the EU market or whose output is used in the EU, regardless of where the provider is based. This gives it de facto global impact similar to GDPR. Particularly affects US and Chinese AI companies operating in EU markets.


### Core Ideas & Positioning

**Core Claim:** The central proposition or value claim this item makes

AI providers must be transparent about what data they used to train their models, respect copyright opt-out mechanisms, and clearly label AI-generated content. The EU AI Act's training data provisions establish the principle that AI development is not exempt from existing rights frameworks — copyright holders retain rights over their works even when used as training data, and the public has a right to know when content is AI-generated. This is the most comprehensive regulatory framework for AI training data worldwide.

**Medium Specificity:** What makes this digitally native? What is specific to digital art about this item vs. art generally?

Directly relevant to digital art. The training data provisions address the core tension in AI art: generative models are trained on millions of artworks, often without consent or compensation. The provisions make this practice legally regulable for the first time. The copyright opt-out requirement (respecting Article 4 of the DSM Directive's text and data mining exception) and the training data summary requirement create new obligations that specifically affect how AI models that generate images, text, music, and video are developed.

**Relation To Attention Economy:** How does this item relate to attention logic? Does it optimize for engagement, resist it, or ignore it?

Disruptive to attention-economy AI. The provisions create friction for AI systems that generate content for engagement (social media content farms, automated marketing, deepfakes). By requiring transparency and copyright compliance, the Act makes attention-economy exploitation of creative works more costly and traceable. However, the provisions do not directly address attention-economy dynamics — they regulate the supply chain (training data) rather than the distribution mechanism (algorithmic amplification).

**Relation To Intention:** Does this serve declared structural needs (intention) or capture engagement (attention)? Or is it infrastructure-neutral?

Strongly intention-aligned. The provisions serve declared structural needs of the creative ecosystem: protecting creator rights, ensuring transparency, establishing accountability. This is regulatory infrastructure that supports intention-based cultural production over attention-based content extraction. The Act explicitly recognizes that unregulated AI training creates systemic risk to creative industries and democratic information environments.


### Market & Economic Dimensions

**Revenue Model:** How it sustains itself financially. Primary sale, secondary royalties, subscription, grants, token, none.

Regulatory framework — does not generate revenue directly. Affects revenue models of AI companies (compliance costs, licensing requirements). Creates potential revenue streams for rights holders (licensing training data). Funds enforcement through EU AI Office budget and national competent authorities. Penalties for non-compliance: up to 3% of global annual turnover or EUR 15 million for general-purpose AI model providers.

**Market Position:** Primary market, secondary market, infrastructure, tool, none. Where in the value chain.

Regulatory infrastructure. Sits above all market participants as a constraint. Defines the rules within which AI art tools, platforms, and markets operate in the EU.

**Price Range:** N/A — regulatory framework, not a product or service.
**Collector Demographics:** Who participates as buyer/collector/patron. Crypto-native, traditional, institutional, mixed.

N/A — applies to all participants in the AI ecosystem. Most directly affects: AI model developers (OpenAI, Stability AI, Midjourney, Google DeepMind), content platforms, creative professionals whose works are used as training data, and downstream users of AI-generated content.


### Practice & Aesthetic Dimensions

**Toolchain:** Primary tools, languages, platforms used. What software/hardware enables this practice?

Not a tool but creates requirements for tools. Affects: AI training pipelines (must implement opt-out compliance), content management systems (must implement AI labeling), generative AI tools (must embed provenance information, compatible with C2PA). Creates demand for new tools: training data auditing systems, copyright compliance checkers, opt-out mechanism implementations (robots.txt, ai.txt, Spawning's Do Not Train registry), AI content detection and labeling systems.

**Relation To Ai:** How it engages with (or resists) generative AI. Tool, medium, subject, threat, irrelevant.

This IS regulation of AI. The training data provisions directly govern how generative AI models are built, what data they can use, and how their outputs must be disclosed. Article 53(1)(c) requires providers to put in place a policy to comply with Union copyright law, in particular to identify and comply with reservations of rights expressed pursuant to Article 4(3) of the DSM Directive. Article 53(1)(d) requires a sufficiently detailed summary of training data content. Article 50 requires AI-generated content to be labeled as such. This is the most significant AI regulation for creative practice globally.

**Liveness:** Static artifact, real-time, performative, evolving, generative, interactive.

Regulatory provisions are living documents in practice — interpreted through enforcement actions, court cases, codes of practice, and guidance. The AI Office's codes of practice (under development in 2025-2026) will elaborate the provisions. Not static: the regulatory interpretation evolves as technology evolves.

**Aesthetic Vocabulary:** What critical/aesthetic language exists for describing this? Is the vocabulary adequate or still forming?

Regulatory/legal: training data transparency, copyright opt-out, text and data mining (TDM) exception, sufficiently detailed summary, machine-readable opt-out, AI-generated content labeling, general-purpose AI model (GPAI), systemic risk, fundamental rights. The vocabulary bridges legal, technical, and creative domains but is primarily legal. The aesthetic implications (how does mandatory AI labeling change the perception of AI art?) lack dedicated critical vocabulary.

**Tendency Axis Position:** Position on A(DAI) tendency axes: openness↔enclosure, commons↔capture, spectacle↔infrastructure, individual↔collective

Openness vs. enclosure: creates obligations for transparency (openness of process) while protecting enclosure rights (copyright). Commons vs. capture: protects commons (public right to know about AI content) while reinforcing private capture (copyright holders' control over training data). Spectacle vs. infrastructure: purely infrastructure. Individual vs. collective: balances individual rights (creator copyright, user transparency) with collective interests (AI innovation, public safety).


### Infrastructure & Governance

**Openness:** Open-source, proprietary, hybrid, CC-licensed. What is shared and what is enclosed?

The Act itself is public law, freely accessible. Codes of practice are developed through multi-stakeholder processes with public consultation. Enforcement decisions will be public. However, the training data summaries required from AI providers may be less transparent than advocates hoped — the detail level of 'sufficiently detailed summary' is contested and subject to codes of practice interpretation.

**Governance Model:** Who decides what. DAO, curatorial, corporate, community, founding-team, expert-committee, none.

EU institutional governance: European Commission, European AI Office (enforcement), European Artificial Intelligence Board (coordination of national authorities), national competent authorities (member state level enforcement). Multi-stakeholder input through codes of practice development, public consultations, and expert groups. Democratic accountability through European Parliament oversight.

**Data Sovereignty:** Who owns/controls the data, art, metadata? Can artists export their data? Is it portable?

The provisions strengthen creator data sovereignty by requiring respect for copyright opt-out and transparency about training data use. Artists and rights holders can assert control over whether their works are used for AI training. However, enforcement is challenging: how do you verify compliance with opt-out at the scale of internet-wide data scraping? The practical effectiveness of data sovereignty depends on technical implementation of opt-out mechanisms and enforcement capacity.

**Interoperability:** Can it connect to other systems/platforms? Standards compliance. API availability. Graph-readiness.

The Act references existing standards (C2PA for AI content labeling, DSM Directive for copyright). It does not create its own technical standards but mandates compliance with outcomes, leaving implementation to providers. This approach allows interoperability with existing systems. The AI Office's codes of practice will further specify technical requirements. The Act is designed to work with, not replace, existing IP frameworks.

**Preservation Strategy:** How permanence is addressed. On-chain, IPFS, institutional archive, none, at-risk.

Training data summaries create a new archival requirement — documented records of what data was used to train models. This has preservation implications: for the first time, there will be a documented record (however summary) of AI models' cultural inputs. The Act does not directly address preservation of AI-generated art, but AI labeling requirements create metadata that supports future preservation and historicization.

**Consent Architecture:** How consent is managed. Binary include/exclude, granular, machine-readable, absent.

Hybrid opt-out. The default under EU copyright law (DSM Directive Article 4) is that text and data mining for commercial purposes requires an opt-out: rights holders must explicitly reserve their rights, or their works can be used. The AI Act reinforces this opt-out framework and requires AI providers to respect it. This is not opt-in consent (artists must actively refuse rather than actively permit). The opt-out approach has been criticized by artist advocacy groups as insufficient — it places the burden on creators to protect their works rather than requiring AI companies to obtain permission.


### Field Position & Gaps

**Relation To Traditional Art World:** Integration, parallel, opposition, absorption, indifference. How does it sit relative to galleries/museums/fairs?

Integration with existing rights frameworks. The Act reinforces traditional copyright principles (artists own their works) and extends them to the AI context. Traditional art world institutions benefit from the protections. The Act does not disrupt the art world — it protects it from AI disruption. Museums, galleries, and collecting societies are stakeholders in the regulatory process.

**What It Enables:** What becomes possible because of this? What can practitioners do that they couldn't before?

Legal basis for artists to control how their works are used in AI training. Transparency requirements that make AI model composition auditable. Content labeling that helps audiences distinguish AI-generated from human-created work. A framework for licensing and compensation for training data use. Precedent for other jurisdictions to follow. Design constraints for any AI-powered creative tool operating in the EU.

**What It Lacks:** What's missing, broken, or structurally absent from this item?

Effective enforcement mechanisms at scale (how to monitor compliance across all AI training globally). Adequate training data summary detail (the 'sufficiently detailed' standard is vague). Retroactive application (existing models trained before the Act are not retroactively regulated). Individual artist compensation mechanism (the Act protects rights but does not create a payment system). Coverage of open-source models (exemptions for open-source complicate enforcement). Adequate resources for national competent authorities to enforce.

**Frontier Signal:** Is this emerging (frontier), established, or declining? If frontier: what category does it challenge?

Established as regulation, frontier in implementation. The Act is law but the practical meaning of the training data provisions is still being determined through codes of practice (2025-2026). The frontier is in implementation: what does 'sufficiently detailed summary' mean in practice? How are opt-out mechanisms technically implemented? How is compliance verified? The answers to these questions in 2026 will determine whether the provisions are transformative or toothless.


### Attention & Intention Dynamics

**Discovery Mechanism:** How people find this. Algorithm, curation, word of mouth, institutional, search, social media, none.

Regulatory compliance requirements (AI companies must discover and implement). Legal press, technology press, art press. EU official publications. Advocacy organizations (European Digital Rights, Communia, artist unions). Conferences and policy forums. Not discovered through social media — discovered through professional and regulatory channels.

**Attention Dependency:** How dependent on platform attention/engagement metrics? Would it survive if Twitter/Instagram disappeared?

Zero. Regulation does not depend on attention or engagement. The Act applies regardless of whether anyone is paying attention to it. Enforcement is institutional, not attention-driven. This is the opposite of attention-economy logic: compliance is mandatory, not voluntary.

**Intention Alignment:** Does it serve declared structural needs of the field or capture engagement? Intention-native, attention-native, neutral.

Maximally intention-aligned. Regulation is the purest form of declared structural need: democratic institutions have determined that AI training data transparency and copyright compliance are necessary for the public good. The provisions exist to serve the field's structural needs, not to capture engagement.

**Commons Contribution:** Does it contribute to shared field knowledge (open data, shared vocabulary, public infrastructure) or enclose it?

Strong. The Act creates new commons: mandatory training data summaries become public knowledge about AI model composition. AI labeling creates a public information layer about content authenticity. The regulatory framework itself is a commons (public law, freely accessible). However, the Act also reinforces private enclosure (copyright) — the tension between commons and enclosure is managed, not resolved.


### Provenance & Temporality

**Provenance Type:** What kind of provenance does this track? Ownership only, meaning, both, neither.

Both, indirectly. The Act requires provenance of AI model training (what data was used — a form of creation provenance) and provenance of AI-generated content (labeling — a form of origin marking). It does not track provenance of meaning, but the training data summaries create a new form of cultural provenance: what cultural inputs produced what AI capabilities.

**Temporal Logic:** Real-time, archival, cyclical/tidal, anticipatory, deep-historical, none.

Regulatory temporality: phased implementation (2024-2026), with ongoing interpretation through enforcement actions and case law. The Act creates temporal obligations: ongoing compliance, regular reporting, evolving codes of practice. For the field, it introduces a temporal marker: pre-Act AI training (unregulated) vs. post-Act AI training (regulated). This temporal divide will shape how AI art is historicized.

**Absence Handling:** Does this item detect, represent, or address what is missing from the field? Or only what is present?

The Act addresses a critical absence: the lack of legal framework for AI training data governance. It makes the previously invisible (AI model composition) partially visible (training data summaries). However, it does not fully address the absence of compensation mechanisms, enforcement capacity, or global coordination. The provisions make certain absences visible (we can now see that training data summaries are inadequate) while creating new ones (global enforcement gaps).


### Coherence & Contestability

**Coherence Vs Consensus:** Does this seek consensus (single truth), coherence (multiple valid readings coexist), or neither?

Consensus-seeking through democratic process. EU legislation seeks political consensus across member states, parliament, and commission (trilogue process). The Act represents negotiated consensus between competing interests: AI industry (wanted minimal regulation), creative industries (wanted strong protections), civil society (wanted transparency and rights), and member states (varying positions). The result is a consensus document with deliberate ambiguities that will be resolved through implementation.

**Contestability:** Can outputs, classifications, or judgments be challenged? By whom? Through what mechanism?

High. The provisions are contestable through: judicial review (CJEU), national court interpretation, legislative amendment, codes of practice negotiation, lobbying, and public advocacy. AI companies are already contesting the scope of training data summary requirements. Artist groups are contesting the adequacy of opt-out protections. The contestation is ongoing and productive.

**Forkability:** Can this be forked — taken, modified, and run independently? What are the practical barriers?

Not forkable in the software sense — regulation is sovereign. However, the regulatory model is exportable: other jurisdictions can adopt similar provisions (and several are developing them). The Act sets a template that can be adapted, strengthened, or weakened by other regulatory systems. In this sense, the EU AI Act is a 'reference implementation' of AI training data regulation.


### A(DAI) Comparison

**Layer Mapping:** substrate
**What Adai Should Adopt:** Specific patterns, methods, or principles A(DAI) should learn from this item.

The training data transparency principle — A(DAI) should make its knowledge sources visible and auditable, exceeding the Act's requirements as a values demonstration. The opt-out compliance infrastructure — A(DAI) must respect creator preferences about data inclusion from the start. The phased implementation approach — complex systems need graduated deployment. The multi-stakeholder governance concept — involving diverse voices in rule-making. The temporal marking concept (pre/post regulation) as a model for field periodization.

**What Adai Should Refuse:** What A(DAI) must explicitly refuse from this item's approach.

The opt-out default — A(DAI) should adopt an opt-in model (explicit consent for inclusion) rather than opt-out (artists must actively refuse). The 'sufficiently detailed summary' vagueness — A(DAI) should provide full, granular transparency about its knowledge sources. The enforcement-gap tolerance — A(DAI) should build compliance into its architecture rather than relying on external enforcement. The exemption for open-source — A(DAI) should hold itself to the highest standard regardless of its licensing model.

**Structural Tension:** The productive tension between this item's approach and A(DAI)'s architecture.

The EU AI Act establishes minimum standards; A(DAI) aspires to model maximum standards. The Act treats consent as opt-out; A(DAI) treats consent as opt-in. The Act regulates corporate AI from the outside; A(DAI) builds consent and transparency from the inside. The productive tension: A(DAI) can use the Act as a baseline while demonstrating what a genuinely consent-first, transparency-maximalist approach looks like. A(DAI) should be the system that makes the EU AI Act's provisions look conservative.


### Regulatory & Legal Environment

**Ip Model:** How intellectual property is handled. CC license, all-rights-reserved, on-chain ownership, public domain, mixed.

The Act reinforces the existing EU copyright framework (DSM Directive) and extends it to AI training contexts. It does not create new IP rights but clarifies that existing copyright applies to AI training data. The TDM exception (Article 4 DSM Directive) allows commercial data mining unless rights holders opt out — the AI Act requires AI providers to implement mechanisms to respect this opt-out. The Act maintains the European tradition of strong moral rights (attribution, integrity).

**Opt In Vs Opt Out:** Is consent opt-in (explicit) or opt-out (must actively refuse)? Neither? What are the implications?

Opt-out. Under the DSM Directive Article 4(3), rights holders must explicitly reserve their rights to prevent commercial text and data mining. The AI Act reinforces this opt-out framework: AI providers must respect rights reservations expressed in 'an appropriate manner, including machine-readable means.' This means artists must actively opt out (using robots.txt, ai.txt, or similar mechanisms) rather than being asked for permission. Artist advocacy groups argue this is inadequate — the burden should be on AI companies to obtain consent, not on artists to refuse.


### Ecosystem Position

**Platform Dependency:** What platforms, chains, or services does this depend on? Single point of failure risk.

No platform dependency — this is sovereign regulation. However, enforcement effectiveness depends on cooperation from platforms and AI providers. The Act applies extraterritorially but enforcement against non-EU entities depends on their EU market presence (similar to GDPR enforcement challenges).

**Network Effects:** Does this benefit from or contribute to network effects? Is it a hub, bridge, or isolate?

Strong regulatory network effects. As EU compliance becomes standard, it raises the baseline globally (the 'Brussels Effect'). AI companies that comply for EU markets often apply the same standards globally (easier than maintaining two versions). Other jurisdictions adopting similar provisions amplify the effect. The regulatory framework creates a gravity well: the more entities comply, the more costly it is to not comply.

**Post Crash Trajectory:** Specific trajectory since 2022-2023 crash. Growing, stable, declining, pivoting, dead.

The Act was developed during and after the NFT crash but is not directly related to crypto markets. It responds to the generative AI boom (2022-present). The post-crash relevance: the NFT crash demonstrated the consequences of unregulated digital asset markets. The AI Act represents a proactive regulatory approach to avoid a similar unregulated boom-and-bust cycle in generative AI. For digital art specifically, the Act arrives at a moment when the field is rebuilding post-crash with greater emphasis on sustainability and rights.

<a name="environmental-critique-of-blockchain-art"></a>
## Environmental critique of blockchain art

### Basic Identification

**Name:** Environmental critique of blockchain art
**Type:** discourse
**Originator:** Key people, organizations, or communities behind this item

Memo Akten (artist/researcher, published seminal analysis on cryptoart.wtf and Medium, 2020-2021), Joanie Lemercier (French artist/climate activist), Mat Dryhurst, Primavera De Filippi, Addie Wagenknecht. Academic: Nature Humanities and Social Sciences Communications (2024 ethical review). Institutional: Ethereum Foundation (The Merge). Open Earth Foundation (CarbonDrop initiative).

**Year:** 2020
**Key Url:** https://memoakten.medium.com/the-unreasonable-ecological-cost-of-cryptoart-2221d3eb2053
**Geography:** Where it operates, originates, or is concentrated

Global discourse, originating primarily in European and North American artist communities. Ethereum Foundation (Switzerland). Tezos community as alternative (France-originated).


### Core Ideas & Positioning

**Core Claim:** The central proposition or value claim this item makes

Blockchain-based art production carries significant environmental costs that the field must account for. Memo Akten's 2020-2021 analysis demonstrated that a single NFT had a carbon footprint of ~340 kWh (211 kg CO2), equivalent to driving 1,000 km. Ethereum's Merge to Proof-of-Stake (September 2022) reduced energy consumption by 99.95%, largely resolving the primary critique but leaving residual materiality questions about infrastructure costs, e-waste, and the environmental accounting of alternative chains.

**Medium Specificity:** What makes this digitally native? What is specific to digital art about this item vs. art generally?

Entirely medium-specific. The environmental critique is about the infrastructure layer of digital art, not the art itself. No equivalent exists in traditional art (a painting does not require continuous network consensus). The critique targets the gap between the immateriality of digital art and the material energy costs of its verification infrastructure. This is a critique of the substrate, not the surface - the hidden costs of seemingly dematerialized cultural production.

**Relation To Attention Economy:** How does this item relate to attention logic? Does it optimize for engagement, resist it, or ignore it?

The environmental critique gained attention through the attention economy it critiqued: Akten's Medium posts went viral, Lemercier's cancellation of NiftyGateway drops was widely reported. The discourse operated within social media attention cycles, sometimes oversimplifying the technical reality. Post-Merge, the environmental critique lost attention despite residual concerns remaining valid. The attention economy amplified the critique during the PoW era and then largely moved on, even though materiality questions persist.

**Relation To Intention:** Does this serve declared structural needs (intention) or capture engagement (attention)? Or is it infrastructure-neutral?

Intention-aligned critique. Artists like Akten and Lemercier were motivated by genuine concern for environmental impact, not engagement metrics. The critique served the field's declared need for ethical infrastructure. However, the critique was also weaponized by bad-faith actors dismissing all crypto art. The intention was to improve infrastructure, not to destroy it; the result was both: the Merge (improvement) and ongoing stigma (damage).


### Market & Economic Dimensions

**Revenue Model:** How it sustains itself financially. Primary sale, secondary royalties, subscription, grants, token, none.

The critique itself has no revenue model. It was produced as public discourse (Medium posts, blog posts, open research). Akten's cryptoart.wtf calculator was free. The CarbonDrop initiative raised funds for Open Earth Foundation through donated artworks. Some researchers received academic funding. The discourse was a commons contribution, not a commercial product.

**Market Position:** Primary market, secondary market, infrastructure, tool, none. Where in the value chain.

Critical infrastructure discourse that influenced market behavior. Lemercier cancelled drops. Some collectors avoided PoW-based NFTs. Tezos gained market share partly due to environmental positioning. The critique functioned as a market signal that redirected some activity from Ethereum (PoW) to lower-energy alternatives. Post-Merge, the market impact has diminished but environmental perception continues to deter some institutional adoption.

**Price Range:** Typical price points for art sold/exhibited, if applicable

Not directly applicable. The critique addressed the cost of participation (gas fees as energy proxy) rather than art prices. Indirectly, environmental stigma may have contributed to the NFT price crash by providing moral justification for market exit.

**Sustainability:** Can this survive without speculative interest? What is the non-hype sustainability model?

The critique contributed to its own resolution: artist pressure was a factor in Ethereum's Merge to PoS. Post-Merge, the environmental critique is largely addressed at the Ethereum level. However, Bitcoin Ordinals (PoW) remain energy-intensive. The broader question of digital infrastructure materiality (data centers, device manufacture, network energy) persists but receives less attention than the blockchain-specific critique.


### Practice & Aesthetic Dimensions

**Toolchain:** Primary tools, languages, platforms used. What software/hardware enables this practice?

Akten used SuperRare API data, Ethereum gas analysis, carbon footprint calculators. Lemercier used personal energy audits and studio consumption data. General tools: Ethereum energy consumption trackers, Digiconomist Bitcoin Energy Index, carbon offset calculators. Post-Merge: Ethereum Foundation energy reporting, green blockchain benchmarking tools.

**Relation To Ai:** How it engages with (or resists) generative AI. Tool, medium, subject, threat, irrelevant.

Increasingly relevant as AI energy costs become the new environmental frontier. Training large language models and image generators consumes substantial energy. The critique methodology developed for blockchain (per-transaction energy accounting, lifecycle analysis) is being adapted to AI inference costs. AI art faces similar materiality questions that the blockchain critique pioneered, though the discourse has not yet reached the same intensity.

**Liveness:** Static artifact, real-time, performative, evolving, generative, interactive.

The critique is a living discourse, evolving with the technology it critiques. The Merge was a real-time resolution event. Ongoing monitoring of alternative chain energy consumption. The discourse has shifted from crisis to ongoing materiality accounting.

**Aesthetic Vocabulary:** What critical/aesthetic language exists for describing this? Is the vocabulary adequate or still forming?

Carbon footprint, proof-of-work, proof-of-stake, gas fees, energy consumption, materiality, dematerialization, ecological cost, green blockchain, carbon offset, The Merge, e-waste. The vocabulary bridges environmental science, blockchain engineering, and art criticism. Akten and Lemercier introduced a materiality vocabulary that did not previously exist in digital art discourse - the language for discussing the physical substrate of seemingly immaterial art.

**Tendency Axis Position:** Position on A(DAI) tendency axes: openness↔enclosure, commons↔capture, spectacle↔infrastructure, individual↔collective

Openness: the critique was conducted openly, with public data and open research. Commons: the critique was a commons contribution (free tools, public analysis). Infrastructure over spectacle: focused on substrate costs rather than surface aesthetics. Collective: driven by collective concern rather than individual benefit. Strongly aligned with commons, infrastructure, and collective tendencies.


### Infrastructure & Governance

**Openness:** Open-source, proprietary, hybrid, CC-licensed. What is shared and what is enclosed?

Highly open. Akten published methods and data openly on Medium. Lemercier published on personal blog. CarbonDrop was collaborative. Cryptoart.wtf was a free public tool. Academic research published in open-access journals. The environmental critique was conducted as open-source knowledge production.

**Governance Model:** Who decides what. DAO, curatorial, corporate, community, founding-team, expert-committee, none.

Community-driven, no formal governance. Artists, researchers, and engineers collaborating informally. The collective guide to eco-friendly crypto art was multi-authored. No organization owned the critique; it was distributed across individual voices. The Ethereum Foundation's decision to implement PoS was partly responsive to this community pressure, representing a rare case of artist-community influence on infrastructure governance.

**Data Sovereignty:** Who owns/controls the data, art, metadata? Can artists export their data? Is it portable?

Data used was publicly available (blockchain data, energy consumption data). Akten's analysis was independently replicable. No proprietary data claims. The critique demonstrated that public blockchain data could be used for environmental accountability - a model for infrastructure auditing.

**Interoperability:** Can it connect to other systems/platforms? Standards compliance. API availability. Graph-readiness.

The critique applied across all PoW blockchains, not just Ethereum. Methodologies transferable to any energy-consuming infrastructure. Post-Merge, the framework extends to comparing energy profiles across chains (Ethereum PoS, Tezos, Solana, Bitcoin PoW). The analytical framework is interoperable even if the specific data is chain-specific.

**Preservation Strategy:** How permanence is addressed. On-chain, IPFS, institutional archive, none, at-risk.

Primary texts preserved on Medium, personal blogs, academic journals, and the Internet Archive. Akten's cryptoart.wtf was taken offline due to harassment, representing a preservation loss. Academic publications provide more durable preservation. The discourse is well-documented but some primary sources are at risk.

**Consent Architecture:** How consent is managed. Binary include/exclude, granular, machine-readable, absent.

The critique itself was about a consent failure: artists and buyers participating in PoW blockchain art were not informed about energy costs. Akten and Lemercier made this invisible cost visible, creating the conditions for informed consent. Post-Merge, the consent question shifts to: are participants adequately informed about residual environmental costs of PoS chains, data center energy, and device lifecycle impacts?


### Field Position & Gaps

**Relation To Traditional Art World:** Integration, parallel, opposition, absorption, indifference. How does it sit relative to galleries/museums/fairs?

The environmental critique provided traditional art world skeptics with a moral argument against blockchain art. Museums cited environmental concerns as reason for slow adoption. The critique also revealed that traditional art's environmental costs (shipping, climate-controlled storage, art fair travel) were unexamined by comparison. The discourse opened a broader conversation about art world environmental responsibility.

**What It Enables:** What becomes possible because of this? What can practitioners do that they couldn't before?

Environmental accountability for digital art infrastructure. Informed consent about participation costs. Migration to lower-energy alternatives (Tezos, Solana, PoS Ethereum). The Merge itself - artist pressure contributed to Ethereum's transition. A methodology for auditing infrastructure materiality that extends beyond blockchain to AI and cloud computing. Critical discourse about the hidden costs of dematerialized cultural production.

**What It Lacks:** What's missing, broken, or structurally absent from this item?

Post-Merge follow-up: the discourse largely stopped after the Merge rather than extending to residual concerns. Comprehensive lifecycle analysis (device manufacture, e-waste, network infrastructure). Comparative analysis with traditional art market environmental costs. Ongoing monitoring rather than one-time critique. Integration with broader digital sustainability frameworks. A nuanced vocabulary for discussing degrees of environmental impact rather than binary acceptable/unacceptable.

**Frontier Signal:** Is this emerging (frontier), established, or declining? If frontier: what category does it challenge?

Established discourse, no longer frontier for blockchain specifically (post-Merge). Frontier edge: extending the critique to AI art energy costs, comprehensive lifecycle analysis of digital art infrastructure, and materiality accounting for cloud services. The methodology is frontier even if the blockchain-specific application is now established.


### Attention & Intention Dynamics

**Discovery Mechanism:** How people find this. Algorithm, curation, word of mouth, institutional, search, social media, none.

Social media (Medium viral posts, Twitter threads), art press coverage, academic publication. Akten's analysis spread through crypto art community first, then mainstream tech and art media. The critique was discovered through the same attention economy it critiqued, using viral mechanisms to surface a structural concern.

**Attention Dependency:** How dependent on platform attention/engagement metrics? Would it survive if Twitter/Instagram disappeared?

High initial attention dependency for impact (needed viral spread to create pressure). Low ongoing dependency: the Merge happened regardless of continued attention. Post-Merge, the discourse persists in academic and institutional contexts without requiring social media attention. The critique successfully translated attention-dependent discovery into attention-independent structural change.

**Intention Alignment:** Does it serve declared structural needs of the field or capture engagement? Intention-native, attention-native, neutral.

Strongly intention-aligned. The critique served the field's structural need for environmental accountability. It was motivated by genuine ethical concern rather than engagement metrics. The CarbonDrop initiative attempted to combine critique with constructive action. The discourse exemplifies how intention-native critique can drive infrastructure change.

**Commons Contribution:** Does it contribute to shared field knowledge (open data, shared vocabulary, public infrastructure) or enclose it?

Significant commons contribution. Public research, open data, free tools, collaborative guides, academic publications. The environmental critique is one of the most significant commons contributions in digital art discourse: it created public knowledge that changed infrastructure decisions. The methodology is reusable for future environmental accountability.


### Provenance & Temporality

**Provenance Type:** What kind of provenance does this track? Ownership only, meaning, both, neither.

Meaning provenance: the critique tracks the ethical and environmental context of art production, not ownership. It adds a layer of meaning provenance to any blockchain-based artwork: when was it minted (PoW era vs. PoS era), on which chain, at what environmental cost? This temporal context becomes part of the work's meaning.

**Temporal Logic:** Real-time, archival, cyclical/tidal, anticipatory, deep-historical, none.

Historical-archival with a clear turning point: pre-Merge (high environmental cost) and post-Merge (dramatically reduced cost). The temporal logic is before/after, with the September 2022 Merge as the dividing line. Works minted in the PoW era carry different environmental provenance than those minted after. Deep-historical: connects to longer history of industrial environmental critique.

**Absence Handling:** Does this item detect, represent, or address what is missing from the field? Or only what is present?

The critique surfaced what was absent from digital art discourse: materiality accounting. It made visible the invisible energy costs that were absent from marketplace interfaces, collector decisions, and institutional evaluations. However, post-Merge, the critique's own absence from active discourse means residual concerns go unaddressed.


### Coherence & Contestability

**Coherence Vs Consensus:** Does this seek consensus (single truth), coherence (multiple valid readings coexist), or neither?

Near-consensus that PoW blockchain art had unacceptable environmental costs. Post-Merge consensus that the primary issue was resolved. Residual disagreement about: whether art NFTs were individually responsible for blockchain energy use (the marginal vs. average cost debate), whether PoS fully resolves the critique, and whether broader materiality concerns remain urgent. Coherence around the principle of environmental accountability, divergence on details.

**Contestability:** Can outputs, classifications, or judgments be challenged? By whom? Through what mechanism?

Highly contested during the PoW era. Crypto maximalists dismissed the critique with arguments about marginal energy costs, renewable energy mining, and comparisons to traditional banking energy use. Akten reported harassment and misinformation campaigns. Post-Merge, contestability has decreased as the primary data point (PoW energy consumption) is no longer relevant for Ethereum. The debate has shifted to more nuanced territory.

**Forkability:** Can this be forked — taken, modified, and run independently? What are the practical barriers?

The analytical methodology is highly forkable: open data, published methods, replicable calculations. The discourse has already been forked to other domains (AI energy consumption, cloud computing). The environmental accountability framework is a reusable public good.


### A(DAI) Comparison

**Layer Mapping:** substrate
**What Adai Should Adopt:** Specific patterns, methods, or principles A(DAI) should learn from this item.

The principle of infrastructure materiality accounting: making visible the hidden costs of digital systems. The methodology of public, open environmental auditing. The insight that dematerialized cultural production has material substrates that must be acknowledged. The practice of extending critique to one's own infrastructure, not just others'. A(DAI) should account for its own infrastructure costs (cloud computing, AI inference) using the framework this critique established.

**What Adai Should Refuse:** What A(DAI) must explicitly refuse from this item's approach.

The binary framing (blockchain art is bad / blockchain art is fixed). The tendency to focus critique on visible targets while ignoring equivalent costs elsewhere. The weaponization of environmental critique as a gatekeeping mechanism. The assumption that reducing energy consumption resolves all materiality questions. A(DAI) should refuse the simplification that energy efficiency equals environmental responsibility.

**Structural Tension:** The productive tension between this item's approach and A(DAI)'s architecture.

A(DAI) is building digital infrastructure that inevitably has material costs (servers, AI inference, network traffic). The environmental critique demands that A(DAI) account for these costs transparently. The tension is between the desire to build commons-first digital infrastructure and the material reality that all digital infrastructure has environmental costs. A(DAI) cannot claim to be infrastructure-aware while ignoring its own substrate costs.


### Regulatory & Legal Environment

**Regulatory Exposure:** Which regulations apply? EU AI Act, AB 2013, DMCA, copyright opt-out regimes. How does this item comply or conflict?

EU sustainability reporting directives may apply to blockchain platforms. EU Taxonomy for sustainable activities is evolving to cover digital infrastructure. Environmental claims about green blockchain must comply with EU Green Claims Directive (proposed). No specific regulation targets the environmental cost of art production on blockchain, but broader ESG frameworks create institutional pressure for environmental accountability.

**Ip Model:** How intellectual property is handled. CC license, all-rights-reserved, on-chain ownership, public domain, mixed.

Not directly applicable. The environmental critique exists in the public domain. Akten's analysis was published under open terms. Academic research follows standard publishing IP models. No proprietary environmental audit methodology emerged.

**Opt In Vs Opt Out:** Is consent opt-in (explicit) or opt-out (must actively refuse)? Neither? What are the implications?

Pre-Merge: implicit opt-in to environmental cost with no opt-out (using Ethereum meant accepting PoW energy consumption). Post-Merge: opt-in to lower-cost PoS. Choice of chain is now an explicit environmental choice (Ethereum PoS vs. Bitcoin PoW vs. Tezos). The critique transformed an invisible involuntary cost into a visible voluntary choice.


### Ecosystem Position

**Platform Dependency:** What platforms, chains, or services does this depend on? Single point of failure risk.

The critique was platform-independent but focused on Ethereum (largest NFT ecosystem). Tezos, Solana, and other PoS chains benefited as alternatives. Post-Merge, platform environmental dependency is dramatically reduced. The critique's impact was mediated through platforms: Lemercier's NiftyGateway cancellation, the CarbonDrop initiative, marketplace energy disclosures.

**Network Effects:** Does this benefit from or contribute to network effects? Is it a hub, bridge, or isolate?

The critique created negative network effects for PoW platforms and positive network effects for PoS alternatives. Tezos art community (Objkt, fxhash) grew partly due to environmental positioning. The discourse also created a network of environmentally-conscious artists, researchers, and organizations (Open Earth Foundation, collaborative guides) that persists as informal infrastructure.

**Post Crash Trajectory:** Specific trajectory since 2022-2023 crash. Growing, stable, declining, pivoting, dead.

The environmental critique peaked in 2021, was largely resolved by the Merge in September 2022, and is now a residual background concern. Post-crash, environmental issues are less salient because the market itself has contracted. Institutional actors still cite environmental concerns when evaluating blockchain art acquisition. The trajectory is declining urgency (resolved primary concern) with emerging relevance (AI energy costs, comprehensive lifecycle analysis). Stable as a historical reference point, pivoting toward broader digital sustainability discourse.
